title: Cap. III Rat. 2: Vasquez — physical vs moral media; no election before works-foresight
pass_a_gloss: Reason 2. Secondly, Vasquez argues from the discrimination of physical and moral means. In physical means he grants that an efficacious intention of the end precedes the intention of the means: but whenever a means to some end is moral (such as good works related to the obtaining of eternal life) he denies that there can be any efficacious will in God of conferring such an end before the foreknowledge of the means: God therefore does not elect to glory except from the foresight of works, In 1. qu. 23. art. 3. disp. 89. ch. 9. See also disp. 81. ch. 5. And that there is such a difference between moral and physical means, he thinks he can show from this: that physical means have in themselves a natural power of causing the end without relation to another's will: therefore even if the end is efficaciously intended before their foreknowledge, nonetheless by their own power, when they are applied, they conduce to obtaining the end. But now, because moral means do not produce the end by an intrinsic and natural power, but from another's ordination, unless by his foresight they are ordained and accepted to the end before that end has been efficaciously intended for someone, they will be of no moment for obtaining the end: and that they may be accepted and ordained, it is necessary that they be foreseen. Therefore there is no predestination of anyone to this end of glory except after foresight of works, which are moral means ordained by God to the same.
pass_b_english: Rat. 2. Second, Vasquez argues from the split between physical and moral means. With physical means he grants that an efficacious intention of the end comes before intending the means. But whenever the means to an end is moral (good works ordered to eternal life), he denies God can have any efficacious will to confer that end before foreknowing the means. So God elects to glory only from foresight of works (In 1. q. 23 art. 3 disp. 89 ch. 9; also disp. 81 ch. 5). He thinks he can prove the difference: physical means carry in themselves a natural power to cause the end, without depending on another's will — so even if the end is intended before they are foreknown, when applied they still tend to the end by their own virtue. Moral means, he says, do not produce the end by any inward natural power but only by another's ordination; unless foresight ordains and accepts them to the end before that end is efficaciously intended for someone, they count for nothing toward obtaining it — and to be accepted and ordained they must be foreseen. Hence no one is predestined to glory's end except after foresight of works that are moral means God ordained to that end.
source_text: Rat. 2. Secundo, argumentatur Vasques a discrimine mediorum Physicorum & Moralium. In Physicis mediis concedit efficacem intentionem finis praecedere intentionem mediorum: at quoties medium ad aliquem finem est morale (qualia sunt opera bona relata ad vitae aeternae consecutionem) negat ullam esse posse efficacem voluntatem in Deo conferendi talem finem ante praescientiam mediorum: Deus ergo non eligit ad gloriam nisi ex praevisione operum, In 1. quaest. 23. art. 3. disp. 89. cap. 9. Vide etiam disp. 81. cap. 5. Esse autem talem differentiam inter media moralia & physica, hinc putat se posse ostendere; quod media physica in se habeant naturalem virtutem causandi finem sine relatione ad voluntatem alterius: ideo licet finis efficaciter intendatur ante praescientiam eorum, ex sua nihilominus virtute, cum adhibentur, conducunt ad finem obtinendum. Jam vero, quia media moralia non producunt finem infra & naturali virtute, sed ex ordinatione alterius, nisi per praescientiam ejus ordinentur & acceptentur ad finem prius quam ille finis efficaciter alicui intentus fuerit, nullius momenti erunt ad finis consecutionem: ut autem acceptentur & ordinentur, praevideri est necesse. Nulla igitur praedestinatio est cujuscunque ad hunc gloriae finem, nisi post praevisionem operum, quae sunt media moralia a Deo ordinata ad eundem.
